case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may lawfully impose import tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), specifically 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), when responding to a declared national emergency.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)) (and, in the consolidated posture referenced in the filings, an additional constitutional nondelegation question is implicated if the statute is read to allow tariffs).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (e.g., Learning Resources and supporting amici such as Washington Legal Foundation and the listed former officials/scholars) argue that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs because § 1702(a)(1)(B) empowers the President to regulate or prohibit certain transactions involving property interests during a national emergency, but it does not grant the distinct, historically legislative power to impose duties/tariffs. They contend tariffs are a quintessential revenue/commerce measure that Congress authorizes through specific tariff statutes (e.g., the tariff schedule and targeted trade laws), and reading IEEPA to silently include tariff power would evade Congress’s carefully cabined trade authorities and separation-of-powers norms. They also emphasize the need for Supreme Court resolution for nationwide certainty and finality given major economic consequences and conflicting lower-court approaches (including jurisdiction/venue fights over whether challenges belong in the CIT/Federal Circuit or district court/D.C. Circuit).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the government in No. 24-1287 and aligned amici in the consolidation posture described) argue that IEEPA’s emergency powers are broad enough to encompass tariff-like measures as a means of ‘regulat[ing]’ or ‘prohibit[ing]’ import-related economic transactions involving foreign interests, particularly in response to unusual and extraordinary foreign threats. They additionally contend that courts should be cautious about second-guessing the President’s emergency determinations and compliance judgments (invoking political-question-type arguments and emphasizing that Congress created mechanisms for political oversight of emergency declarations). In the consolidated case posture referenced (Nos. 24-1287 & 25-250), they also raise threshold procedural/jurisdictional issues (including whether the Court should reach merits now and which court has exclusive jurisdiction), and, if IEEPA is construed to permit tariffs, the government seeks review of whether that construction is constitutionally permissible (including potential delegation concerns).
key_precedents: K Mart (referenced in oral argument as a Court of International Trade/Federal Circuit exclusive-jurisdiction-type precedent under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i))

BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (referenced for the proposition that congressional ‘ratification’/acquiescence is a weak interpretive basis absent settled, uniform precedent)
Tett (a D.D.C. decision referenced by the government as involving similar political-question/justiciability reasoning)
International Labor (a D.D.C. case referenced for the rule that ‘arising under’ analysis turns on the substantive legal theory, not merely the APA or the tariff schedule)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 1702(a)(1)(B) empowers the President to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property,” and a tariff can be cast as a regulatory condition on entry. But as Justice Kagan persuasively stresses, accepting that reading would collapse IEEPA into a general tariff statute and disrupt Congress’s detailed, carefully cabined tariff scheme in Title 19—exactly the sort of transformative delegation we should not infer from general emergency language. Justice Thomas’s Youngstown framing reinforces the institutional point: absent unmistakable textual authorization to impose “duties/imposts,” the President is not executing Congress’s policy but claiming a quintessentially legislative power by implication. A narrow statutory holding—IEEPA does not authorize import duties under § 1702(a)(1)(B)—resolves the case without reaching broader constitutional questions and best preserves predictable lines between sanctions regulation and tariff-setting.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s authority to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property” can include tariff-like exactions—fails under ordinary public meaning and statutory context: in 1977, “regulate” did not naturally convey a power to impose “duties” or set “rates,” terms Congress uses when it means to authorize revenue measures. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about the statute’s coherence with Congress’s detailed Title 19 tariff regime underscores that we should not treat IEEPA as a silent alternative tariff code, especially where Congress elsewhere cabins tariff delegations with procedures and limits. Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown framing further confirms that, absent unmistakable authorization, the President’s claim amounts to exercising Article I’s duty-setting power by implication—precisely what separation of powers forbids. I therefore remain with the petitioner and would hold that § 1702(a)(1)(B) does not authorize imposing tariffs or tariff-like duties.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument—that IEEPA’s power to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property” includes conditioning entry on payment—still asks us to treat a sanctions-and-blocking statute as a silent tariff statute, which is a bridge too far under ordinary meaning and statutory context. Chief Justice Roberts’s major-questions framing usefully crystallizes why that move is implausible: a generally applicable, revenue-raising tariff is a transformative assertion of power that Congress would be expected to confer unmistakably, especially given the detailed tariff architecture elsewhere. Justice Thomas’s Youngstown point reinforces that, absent clear textual authorization, the President is not executing a delegated power but effectively exercising Article I’s duty-setting function by inference. I therefore remain with petitioner on narrow statutory grounds, which also avoids unnecessary nondelegation/separation-of-powers strain.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that IEEPA’s power to “regulate” import-related transactions involving foreign property necessarily includes conditioning entry on payment—still reads like an effort to turn a sanctions-and-blocking statute into a freestanding tariff code, without the clear congressional statement we should demand for a sweeping, consumer-facing economic measure. Chief Justice Roberts’s major-questions framing (his West Virginia v. EPA analogy) reinforces that we should hesitate before discovering transformative trade-and-revenue authority in general emergency language, especially given Congress’s detailed tariff regime elsewhere. Justice Thomas’s Youngstown point is decisive for me: absent unmistakable statutory authorization, the President is not executing Congress’s will but effectively exercising Article I’s duty-setting power by implication. The practical burdens of broad tariffs on ordinary people and small businesses further underscore why Congress—not the Executive—must speak plainly when authorizing such a blunt instrument.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual move is that IEEPA’s authority to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property” could include conditioning entry on payment, but that reading ignores Congress’s consistent choice to speak in unmistakable “duties/imposts/rates” terms when it means tariff power and would make IEEPA an end-run around Title 19’s detailed tariff framework. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about a clear-statement expectation for transformative economic measures strengthens, rather than substitutes for, the statutory-coherence problem: it is implausible Congress silently created a parallel, unbounded tariff regime inside an emergency sanctions statute. Justice Barrett’s reminder that historical practice or acquiescence cannot supply missing textual authorization is decisive under a pragmatic textualist approach because workability comes from administrable statutory boundaries, not executive gloss that destabilizes the trade/sanctions line. With Justice Thomas’s Youngstown framing in the background, the narrower construction—IEEPA authorizes transaction controls and blocking, not general import duties—remains the better reading and avoids unnecessary constitutional strain.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that IEEPA’s power to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property” can include conditioning entry on payment—still asks us to treat general emergency-transaction language as a silent delegation of the quintessentially legislative power to impose duties. Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-coherence point strengthens my view: Congress has erected a detailed tariff regime using unmistakable terms (“duties,” “imposts,” “rates”) and procedural constraints, making it textually implausible that IEEPA smuggles in a parallel, unbounded tariff authority. Justice Thomas’s Youngstown framing is also decisive: where Congress has occupied the field with specific trade statutes, an implied emergency tariff power pushes the President into Jackson Category 3 absent clear authorization. Even if “regulate” could bear a broad meaning in isolation, constitutional avoidance and the major-questions principle counsel the narrower, ordinary public-meaning reading that keeps IEEPA in its sanctions/asset-control lane.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that IEEPA’s power to “regulate” import-related transactions involving foreign property could, as a practical matter, include conditioning entry on payment. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, that interpretation would quietly transform a sanctions/asset-control statute into a general tariff statute despite Congress’s detailed, cabined trade and tariff schemes elsewhere—an institutional red flag that calls for a clear statement, not inference from broad emergency language. Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—that § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s authority to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property” necessarily includes imposing a tariff as a condition of entry—still fails on ordinary public meaning and statutory context: “regulate” in IEEPA’s sanctions-and-blocking framework does not naturally carry the revenue-exaction connotation Congress historically signals with “duties,” “imposts,” or “tariff” language. Chief Justice Roberts’s major-questions framing usefully reinforces (rather than substitutes for) the textual point: an across-the-board tariff is a transformative economic and fiscal measure, and we should not locate that power in general emergency words when Congress has built detailed tariff delegations elsewhere. Justice Thomas’s Youngstown analysis is also persuasive as a structural backstop—without clear statutory authorization, this looks like the President asserting Article I’s duty-setting power by implication, which constitutional avoidance counsels us not to endorse. Past practice or acquiescence cannot supply the missing textual hook, so I remain with the petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that IEEPA’s power to “regulate” import-related “transactions” involving foreign “property” can be stretched to cover a tariff as a condition on entry. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that reading would transform a targeted emergency economic-controls statute into a sweeping, revenue-raising tariff authority—something Congress ordinarily confers with clear “duties/imposts/rates” language and with procedural constraints embedded in the trade statutes. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence concern is decisive for me as a progressive pragmatist: allowing IEEPA to operate as an unbounded alternative tariff track would evade the accountability and procedural safeguards Congress built elsewhere, with predictable downstream burdens on consumers and small businesses. Youngstown’s requirement of identifiable congressional authorization, emphasized by Justice Thomas, reinforces that ambiguity here cannot be resolved by inference in favor of a core Article I power shift.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” transactions and dealings in “property” in which a foreign country or national has an interest, but it does not clearly confer the distinct and historically legislative power to impose import duties; reading “regulate” to include tariffs would be a dramatic expansion of emergency authority with major economic and political consequences absent unmistakable congressional authorization. As in West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022), we have reason to hesitate before concluding Congress meant to authorize such a transformative trade measure through broad, general language rather than through the specific tariff statutes Congress has enacted. That narrower reading also avoids serious constitutional questions about delegation and protects institutional legitimacy by respecting Congress’s central role over tariffs and revenue measures. Given the jurisdictional disputes, I would resolve the case on the narrowest available statutory ground: IEEPA does not authorize tariffs under § 1702(a)(1)(B).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” but it nowhere speaks in the language of “duties,” “tariffs,” or “imposts”—terms the Constitution assigns to Congress in Article I. Reading IEEPA to include a freestanding power to impose import tariffs would stretch “regulate” beyond its ordinary public meaning in 1977 and effectively transfer Congress’s taxing and foreign-commerce powers without clear textual authorization. Under Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, absent clear congressional authorization the President may not seize legislative power; here, the asserted tariff authority is not clearly conferred by § 1702 and thus cannot be sustained as an exercise of executive power. Any contrary construction would also raise serious constitutional concerns under the nondelegation principle, further counseling against it under a textually faithful reading.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: IEEPA’s text in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving property in which a foreign country or national has an interest, but it does not clearly confer the distinct power to impose across-the-board import duties—an Article I power to “lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises” and to “regulate Commerce with foreign Nations.” Under Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, the President’s power “must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself,” and here the asserted tariff authority lacks the kind of clear congressional authorization one would expect for a measure with sweeping economic and revenue consequences. Reading IEEPA to include tariff power would also raise serious constitutional nondelegation concerns by effectively allowing the Executive to set major trade tax policy without a clear limiting principle, so the better textual reading avoids that. Practical consequences reinforce this conclusion: allowing tariffs by implication under a sanctions statute would destabilize the carefully cabined trade regime Congress enacted elsewhere and shift major policy choices from Congress to the President.

To avoid serious constitutional nondelegation concerns in the consolidated posture, the better construction is that § 1702(a)(1)(B) does not silently confer tariff authority absent a clear statement from Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: IEEPA’s text, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign property interests during an emergency, but it does not speak in the historically distinct terms Congress uses when it confers tariff (duty/impost) authority—especially against the backdrop of Congress’s detailed and pervasive tariff regime in Title 19. Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: IEEPA’s text authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” certain transactions involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), but it does not speak in the language Congress has historically used to confer tariff authority—i.e., to “lay and collect” duties or to set rates on imports—and we should not lightly infer so weighty a power from silence. Under Youngstown, imposing import duties absent clear statutory authorization places the President at least in Justice Jackson’s Category 2 and likely Category 3 where Congress has legislated extensively in the tariff field through specific trade statutes, making implied emergency tariff power especially suspect. Reading IEEPA to allow tariffs would also raise serious separation-of-powers and nondelegation concerns by transferring Congress’s Article I power over “Duties” and foreign commerce to the Executive without clear, bounded guidance, and the Court should avoid such a construction where the text does not compel it. Whatever the wisdom of tariffs as policy, the question is who decides, and on this record Congress has not clearly authorized the President to do so through IEEPA.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: IEEPA § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified transactions involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” but it does not clearly confer the distinct, historically legislative power to impose import duties—an authority the Constitution assigns to Congress, and that Congress has addressed in detailed tariff statutes. Reading this general emergency-transaction authority to silently include tariff power would be a major expansion with large economic consequences, undermining settled separation-of-powers practice and creating serious nondelegation pressure without a clear statement from Congress. Under Youngstown, absent a clear delegation, the President’s unilateral tariffing power sits on the weakest footing given Congress’s traditional and specific control over tariffs and duties. Practical workability and institutional legitimacy also favor a narrow, text- and history-grounded reading that preserves Congress’s primacy over tariff policy and avoids turning IEEPA into a general tariff statute.

Under Youngstown, the President must point to either constitutional power or clear congressional authorization for such an economically and politically significant measure; without clear tariff authorization in IEEPA, the action falls outside Congress’s grant and cannot be sustained. Sawyer, the President must identify authority in an act of Congress or the Constitution, and stretching § 1702(a)(1)(B) to encompass tariffs risks moving from statutory implementation into effectively lawmaking—especially given the major economic consequences and separation-of-powers concerns. If Congress intends to authorize emergency tariffs, it can do so explicitly; courts should not supply that power by inference from general language.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) authorizes a President to impose import tariffs as an emergency economic measure.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (IEEPA), and (as a related constitutional backdrop) the Constitution’s allocation of tariff and taxing powers to Congress (U.S. Const. art. I, § 8; nondelegation principles).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Learning Resources, et al.) argue that IEEPA does not confer authority to impose tariffs because tariffs are a distinct form of revenue-raising/import regulation traditionally reserved to Congress and governed by specific tariff statutes; they contend § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes regulation or prohibition of certain financial/economic transactions to address emergencies, not the unilateral creation of a tariff schedule or generally applicable import duties. They also emphasize the need for Supreme Court resolution to provide nationwide certainty and to prevent end-runs around Congress’s detailed tariff framework.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the President/government) argue that IEEPA’s broad emergency powers—especially the authority to 'regulate' or 'prohibit' specified economic transactions involving foreign commerce and property interests—are sufficiently expansive to encompass tariffs as a tool to counter an 'unusual and extraordinary threat.' They also suggest courts should not second-guess the President’s emergency determinations (invoking political-question-like reasoning), and raise threshold issues (including jurisdiction/venue questions involving the Court of International Trade) that could limit or channel judicial review.
key_precedents: K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc.
BP p.l.c. v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that IEEPA’s authorization to “regulate … importation” could be read to include conditioning entry on payment, but that construction would silently convert a sanctions-and-asset-control statute into a generally applicable tariff code—an Article I function Congress delegates (when it does) in unmistakably tariff-specific terms. Justice Gorsuch’s clear-statement/Youngstown framing is persuasive under a minimalist approach: without words like “duties” or a tariff-rate framework, we should not infer a delegation that bypasses Congress’s comprehensive trade statutes, placing the President’s claim at least near Category 3. Justice Kavanaugh’s coherence point reinforces that reading IEEPA this broadly would create an end-run around Title 19, a major structural shift we should avoid absent clear text. A narrow statutory holding that IEEPA does not authorize generally applicable tariff schedules resolves the case without reaching constitutional questions and best protects institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that a tariff can be characterized as a means to “regulate … importation,” but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, IEEPA never uses the ordinary tariff vocabulary (“duties,” “imposts,” “tariffs”) that would unmistakably signal a delegation of Congress’s core Article I revenue power. Text and structure cut against respondent: §1702 is written in sanctions-and-blocking terms aimed at controlling particular transactions and property interests, not establishing generally applicable border-duty schedules that displace Congress’s comprehensive Title 19 scheme. Under my separation-of-powers analysis, the absence of clear statutory authorization places the President’s claim at Youngstown’s “lowest ebb,” and any ambiguity must be resolved against reading emergency words to effect a structural transfer of the taxing power. No colleague has supplied precedent that compels treating IEEPA as a tariff statute, so I remain with petitioners.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that IEEPA’s power to “regulate” importation and transactions in foreign exchange/property could include conditioning entry on payment, but that interpretation would silently convert a sanctions-and-blocking statute into a general tariff authority—something Congress typically confers using unmistakable tariff language (“duties,” “imposts,” rate schedules). Chief Justice Roberts’s point is decisive for me: §1702(a)(1)(B) lacks any clear textual hook for revenue-raising border exactions, and reading “regulate” to do that much work would create an end-run around Congress’s detailed trade statutes, pushing the claim toward Youngstown’s weakest footing. Justice Gorsuch’s structural/canon point reinforces that any ambiguity should be resolved against reallocating core Article I taxing power via broad emergency phrasing. The practical consequences—IEEPA becoming a freestanding tariff code usable whenever an emergency is declared—confirm that the better reading limits IEEPA to transaction controls and blocking, not generally applicable import duties.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that IEEPA’s power to “regulate … importation” and transactions in foreign property interests can include a border charge as a means of regulation, but that interpretation would silently convert a sanctions-and-asset-control statute into a general tariff code. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively underscore the absence of the tariff-specific vocabulary (“duties,” “imposts,” rate schedules) Congress routinely uses when delegating Article I revenue measures, which triggers a clear-statement requirement before we bless such a major power shift. Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown framing reinforces that, given Congress’s comprehensive trade/tariff enactments, the President’s claim is at best Category 2 and plausibly Category 3 if it functionally displaces Congress’s tariff judgments; ambiguity should cut against the Executive. The real-world burdens of broad emergency tariffs on consumers and small businesses further counsel caution and make me unwilling to infer this authority from general language.

Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-coherence concern sharpens the problem: reading IEEPA to authorize generally applicable tariff schedules would functionally let the Executive bypass Congress’s detailed trade statutes, and under Youngstown that absence of clear authorization, in a field Congress has comprehensively legislated, resolves the case for petitioner without reaching constitutional questions. I therefore stay with petitioner on a narrow statutory holding that IEEPA does not clearly authorize tariff-setting.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: IEEPA’s text, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” certain transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests to meet an “unusual and extraordinary threat,” but it does not clearly delegate the quintessentially legislative power to impose generally applicable import duties—an area the Constitution assigns to Congress in Article I, § 8. Under Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer and Justice Jackson’s framework, sweeping tariffs that effectively tax Americans and restructure trade policy fall at least into a zone requiring clear congressional authorization; absent such clarity, the President cannot rely on emergency rhetoric to supply what the statute and Constitution withhold. Reading IEEPA to allow across-the-board tariffs would also raise serious nondelegation and democratic-accountability concerns, transforming an emergency-sanctions statute enacted to cabin presidential power into a broad tariff code. Given the real-world burdens such tariffs impose on consumers and small businesses—costs borne most heavily by vulnerable households—this Court should require an unmistakable statement from Congress before permitting such an expansive, revenue-raising measure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: IEEPA’s operative grant in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, credit, and “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” but it does not clearly speak to imposing generally applicable import duties—an Article I “Duties, Imposts and Excises” function Congress has addressed through detailed, trade-specific statutes. Reading “regulate … importation” to include creating tariff schedules as an emergency measure would stretch IEEPA beyond its coherent sanctions-focused design and create serious structural and nondelegation concerns; under Youngstown’s framework, absent clear congressional authorization, the President’s unilateral tariff-setting is at best in Justice Jackson’s Category 2 and risks drifting toward Category 3 when it displaces Congress’s chosen tariff framework. Workability and statutory coherence also favor petitioners: allowing tariffs under IEEPA would invite end-runs around the trade laws and make emergency powers a general substitute for Congress’s tariff judgments. Venue/jurisdiction channeling questions cannot cure the merits problem where the asserted power lacks a clear textual foothold in § 1702(a)(1)(B).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: IEEPA’s text authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B); it nowhere speaks in the language of “duties,” “imposts,” or “tariffs,” and we do not lightly read a vague grant of emergency authority to effect so fundamental a shift in the power to tax. The Constitution assigns tariff and revenue authority to Congress, U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, and Youngstown teaches that when the President acts without clear statutory authorization in an area where Congress has legislated, his power is at its “lowest ebb,” counseling against implied tariff power here. Given Congress’s detailed tariff statutes elsewhere and IEEPA’s narrower focus on blocking and regulating transactions, the President’s claim falls at best into Youngstown Category 2 and more plausibly Category 3, defeating the asserted authority absent an unmistakable delegation. Any residual ambiguity in a statute touching the taxing power and separation of powers should be resolved against such a sweeping executive claim, not in favor of it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: IEEPA’s text, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, banking, and property interests to address an “unusual and extraordinary threat,” but it does not clearly speak in the distinct language of “duties” or “tariffs” nor supply the kind of bounded tariff framework Congress has enacted elsewhere in Title 19. Given Article I’s assignment to Congress of the power to “lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises” and to regulate foreign commerce, reading IEEPA to allow generally applicable import duties would be a major expansion with significant separation-of-powers implications that requires clear congressional authorization. Under Youngstown, absent such clear authorization—and especially in light of Congress’s detailed tariff statutes—this looks at best like Justice Jackson’s Category 2 and more plausibly Category 3 if it effectively circumvents Congress’s chosen tariff schemes. Practical workability and institutional legitimacy also favor requiring Congress to speak clearly before emergency powers are used to create broad revenue-raising/import-duty regimes nationwide.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: IEEPA’s operative grant in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests, but its text does not speak in the distinct terms Congress has historically used when conferring tariff authority—i.e., the imposition of “duties” or “imposts” of general applicability at the border. Given the Constitution’s assignment of the power to “lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises” to Congress (Art. I, § 8), we should not infer so consequential a delegation from general language about regulating transactions, especially where Congress has enacted detailed, specific tariff statutes elsewhere in Title 19. Under Youngstown, the President has no independent power to impose tariffs, so any such power must be clearly delegated; IEEPA’s text and structure do not provide that clear authorization. Precedent emphasizing fidelity to statutory text (e.g., K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc.) reinforces that courts must not expand an agency or executive’s authority beyond the statute’s best reading.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: IEEPA’s text authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), but it does not clearly delegate Congress’s distinct tariff power under Article I, § 8 to impose generally applicable import duties for revenue or broad trade policy. Under Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, the President’s authority must stem from Congress or the Constitution, and reading IEEPA to permit tariff schedules would create a major shift in the constitutional allocation of taxing and tariff authority without a clear statement, raising serious nondelegation and separation-of-powers concerns. Procedurally and practically, allowing tariffs via emergency declaration risks end-runs around Congress’s detailed tariff statutes and undermines predictable, reviewable standards for affected importers. Any threshold channeling of review to specialized forums cannot expand substantive power that the statute does not grant.
